name: Citric acid
lead: Citric acid is a weak organic acid found naturally in citrus fruits and an intermediate in the Krebs (tricarboxylic acid) cycle.[1][6] It is widely used as a food acidulant (E330 in the EU) and, in cosmetics, mainly as a pH adjuster and stabiliser; it is also classed as an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) and appears as an active ingredient in some chemical peels.[1][2][7]

People encounter it in skin care in two ways. In most creams, gels and cleansers it is a background ingredient that sets the formula's acidity so other ingredients work and stay stable. In exfoliating products it acts as an AHA, loosening the dead surface layer of skin so the complexion looks smoother and brighter, similar to better-known AHAs such as glycolic and lactic acid.[1][7]

Pure citric acid is a skin and eye irritant, and concentrated solutions can cause redness and pain.[1] No completed controlled trials of citric acid as a stand-alone skin lightening or resurfacing agent have been published.

paras: Citric acid (2-hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic acid) is a triprotic acid with pKa values of about 3.1, 4.8 and 6.4, very soluble in water, and its citrate form binds metal ions, making it a chelating agent.[1][2] It forms colourless, odourless crystals with a sour taste, and its salts include sodium, potassium and calcium citrate.[2]

In the body it is a central metabolite: citrate is formed and consumed in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, which oxidises nutrients to power cells, and a 2023 review in the Journal of Biological Chemistry describes the regulation of that cycle and the history of its discovery.[6]

The Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated pure citric acid from lemon juice in 1784, using lime to precipitate calcium citrate and sulfuric acid to release the acid.[1][2] Until the early twentieth century it was extracted from citrus fruit, a costly process.

In 1917 the American food chemist James Currie showed that strains of the fungus Aspergillus niger could produce citric acid efficiently by fermentation; Pfizer began large-scale production in 1923, and fermentation now accounts for most of global supply.[1][2][8] Reviews describe the fungi Aspergillus niger and Yarrowia lipolytica as the main producers and detail the industrial and cosmetic uses.[8][9]

In creams, gels and liquids it serves as an acidulant to adjust pH.[1][2] Grokipedia lists cosmetics among its applications as a pH adjuster and stabiliser, alongside food, pharmaceutical and detergent uses.[2]

As an AHA it is an active in chemical peels.[1] Wikipedia describes AHAs as used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation, and reports that the FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel have considered AHAs safe when sold at low concentrations, at a pH above 3.5, and with safety instructions. The most common side effects it lists are mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA advised caution about sun exposure after an industry-sponsored study found AHAs can raise the likelihood of sunburn, an effect that is reversible when use stops.[7] The article does not discuss citric acid specifically in this context.

Citric acid is also relevant to the look of teeth. Dental research uses citric acid solutions to create erosion in enamel and dentin specimens so that protective gels can be compared, as in a randomised laboratory study that eroded specimens with 1 percent citric acid and compared fluoride- and stannous-containing gels.[10] Repeated exposure to acidic drinks and foods containing citric acid is discussed as a source of enamel erosion.[1]
A pilot randomised trial registered for 2026 will examine adjunctive acids in gingival melanin depigmentation and its esthetic outcomes.[4]

Pure citric acid is a skin and eye irritant, and repeated exposure may erode tooth enamel.[1] It carries GHS "Warning" labelling for skin and eye irritation.[1] It is classed as generally recognised as safe for food use by the US FDA.[2] In its medical anticoagulant formulation, citrate toxicity can occur with infusion of citrate-containing blood products, starting with tingling around the mouth or extremities.[3]

No studies found of citric acid used alone as a skin lightening agent or peel. Registered trials involve other settings, such as a pilot trial of adjunctive acids in gingival melanin depigmentation (not yet recruiting) and dental implant and kidney stone studies.[4][5]

card.summary: A common food acid and cosmetic pH adjuster that is also an AHA peel ingredient, with little skin-specific trial data.

quick.overview:
Citric acid occurs in citrus fruit and is used everywhere from food to cleaning products. In skin care it mainly adjusts formula pH, and it is also listed among alpha hydroxy acids used in peels.

No controlled trials of citric acid alone as a lightening or resurfacing agent were found.
quick.mechanism: As an AHA it is an acid that can exfoliate; as a buffer it sets product pH, and its citrate form binds metal ions.
quick.risks: Pure citric acid irritates skin and eyes at concentration, and repeated exposure can erode tooth enamel. It is GRAS in the US and E330 in the EU as a food additive.

chain: Applied in a peel, serum or cleanser at low pH
Acid loosens the bonds holding dead surface cells together
angle.text: As an AHA, citric acid is used for gentle surface exfoliation, and as a formulation acid it keeps other skin-care actives at a workable pH. Its direct effect on how skin looks is surface smoothing; as a pH adjuster it supports the products around it.
